prompt: Match each role to what it works on.

pairs.right: the line in front of them
where the function is going next

prompt: What happens to a pair that never swaps roles, by the lesson?

choices.text: It gets faster, since each person specialises in one role
choices.why: Specialising here means one of them stops participating.

choices.text: Nothing; swapping is a matter of taste
choices.why: The lesson treats it as what keeps both engaged.

choices.text: The navigator learns more than the driver
choices.why: Not the lesson's point.

choices.text: It becomes one person working and one watching
choices.why: Right: the watcher's attention drifts within minutes.

prompt: In strong-style pairing, Lívia has an idea for the next step. Who types it?

choices.text: Whoever is faster at typing
choices.why: Typing speed is not the rule.

choices.text: Nobody until they agree on it
choices.why: They try it, which is often faster than agreeing.

choices.text: Diego
choices.why: Right: she navigates and has to explain it well enough for his hands.

choices.text: Lívia, since it is her idea and she knows it best
choices.why: That is the pattern strong style reverses.

prompt: Why is pairing more tiring than working alone?

choices.text: Because pairs work longer hours
choices.why: The lesson suggests pairing for a few hours a day, not longer days.

choices.text: Concentrating aloud, together
choices.why: Right: which is why most teams pair a few hours a day, with breaks.

choices.text: Because one person does all the typing
choices.why: They swap.

choices.text: Because the screens are smaller
choices.why: Not the reason.

prompt: In Cockburn and Williams's study, pairs spent about what percentage more total effort?
hint: And produced about that much fewer defects.

prompt: What did Hannay's 2009 meta-analysis add to the picture?

choices.text: Remote pairs did better than pairs at one desk
choices.why: Not what the lesson reports.

choices.text: Modest, and it depended on the task
choices.why: Right: real but modest effects, most help on complex tasks and with less experienced programmers.

choices.text: Pairing doubles productivity on every task
choices.why: The effects were modest and depended on the task.

choices.text: Pairing has no measurable effect at all
choices.why: The effects were real, if modest.

prompt: When does the lesson say to pair? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four reasons to pair, three not to.

choices.text: Reading a large codebase to understand it
choices.why: No: that is done alone, then discussed.

choices.text: Somebody is new to the team
choices.why: Yes: the fastest onboarding there is.

choices.text: Only one person understands the code
choices.why: Yes: spread the knowledge.

choices.text: A simple configuration change
choices.why: No: simple and well understood.

choices.text: The task is hard or risky
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: What cost of not pairing does the lesson say people forget?

choices.text: Junior engineers leaving because they feel unsupported
choices.why: Possibly true, and not the cost the lesson names.

choices.text: Learning lone-expert code under pressure
choices.why: Right: code only one person knows, learnt when that person is away; pairing moves that cost earlier and makes it smaller.

choices.text: The cost of the screen-sharing tool
choices.why: Not mentioned.

choices.text: The 15% extra effort on the day
choices.why: That is the visible cost of pairing.

prompt: What is the worst remote pairing setup, by the lesson?

choices.text: One person shares the screen, the other watches
choices.why: Right: the navigator cannot point and swaps become slow, so nobody swaps.

choices.text: Both people on headsets without video
choices.why: Many pairs turn video off and do well.

choices.text: A shared editing session in the editor
choices.why: That is what works.

choices.text: A short-lived branch pushed on every swap
choices.why: Fine, if the push and pull take one command.

prompt: By the lesson's test, a swap should take less than how many seconds?
What do the last five minutes of a remote pairing session go to?

choices.text: Booking the next session
choices.why: Useful, but not the point made.

choices.text: A retrospective on how the pairing went, with a score
choices.why: Not what the lesson describes for pairs.

choices.text: What was done, what is next, what was decided
choices.why: Right: so the pair can resume without reconstructing yesterday.

choices.text: Merging whatever is done, finished or not
choices.why: Merging unfinished work is not the advice.

choices.text: A meeting to decide how a task will be split
choices.why: A mob writes the code, not a plan.

choices.text: The whole team on one task at one screen, rotating the driver
choices.why: Right: everybody else navigates.

choices.text: Several pairs working on related tasks in parallel
choices.why: That is pairing, in several places.

choices.text: A review in which the whole team comments on one pull request
choices.why: A review happens after the code is written.

prompt: Put the parts of a mob session in order.
items: Agree the task and the timer
The first driver types what the navigators decide
The driver rotates when the timer ends

prompt: Five engineers mobbed on the outbox reader for two days. How many engineer-days is that?
Which task fits mob programming best, by Marola's pattern?
hint: The whole team will maintain it.

choices.text: A copy fix on the home screen
choices.why: Simple, well understood work.

choices.text: Upgrading a library version across the services
choices.why: Routine work; a mob replaces nothing there.

choices.text: A first version everybody will maintain
choices.why: Right: the outbox reader was mobbed for two days.

choices.text: A week-long feature, start to finish, every day
choices.why: More than about three hours a day left people too tired.

prompt: Diego writes a loop Lívia can see will not work. By their rules, what does she do?

choices.text: Tells him immediately what is wrong
choices.why: Being told teaches him that she found it.

choices.text: Waits a minute or so for the test to show it
choices.why: Right: unless it is costing more than a few minutes.

choices.text: Says nothing at all and lets him commit it
choices.why: The rule is to let it run briefly, not forever.

choices.text: Takes the keyboard and fixes it
choices.why: Then she found it, not him.

prompt: Which are signs a teaching pair is going wrong? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Neither is talking
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The junior stops asking
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The session runs slower than the senior alone would
choices.why: That is expected, and the trade the lesson accepts.

choices.text: The senior is typing
choices.why: Yes: hand the keyboard back.

prompt: What did Lívia do with Diego's "why is it like this?" questions?
hint: Each was one of two things.

choices.text: Took them as a sign he was not ready for the task
choices.why: Most were good questions with good answers.

choices.text: Kept a list; four became small pull requests
choices.why: Right: some showed where the code needed a comment, a rename or a test.

choices.text: Answered each one on the spot and moved on with the task
choices.why: She answered, and also noticed what the questions said about the code.

choices.text: Asked him to save them for their mentoring check-in
choices.why: Questions during pairing are the point of pairing.

prompt: Only Paulo understands the zone service's release script, and he goes on holiday in three weeks. What does this lesson suggest?

choices.text: Mob the whole team on it for a full week
choices.why: More than the task needs, and more than a team can sustain.

choices.text: Pair him with someone on the next releases, strong style
choices.why: Right: knowledge goes through somebody else's hands before it is needed.

choices.text: Freeze releases of the zone service until he is back
choices.why: That avoids the risk by stopping the work.

choices.text: Ask Paulo to write thorough documentation of the script before he leaves
choices.why: Useful, and a handover document is what pairing tends to make unnecessary.
